text_blocks.snippet: The total annual cost of diabetes in the US, including direct medical costs and lost productivity, was $412.9 billion in 2022. Out-of-pocket costs for individuals with diabetes can range from $3,300 to $4,600 per year, even with insurance. These costs include prescription medications, doctor visits, supplies, and potential lost wages. For those with chronic complications or without insurance, costs can be significantly higher.

list.snippet: Additional costs for chronic complications: $470 per year on average.
Potential additional costs for emergency room visits, hospital stays, or home health: $590 for diabetes and $320 for chronic complications.

list.title: Type of diabetes:
list.snippet: Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes have different management needs and costs.

list.title: Insurance coverage:
list.snippet: Those with insurance may still face high out-of-pocket costs, while those without insurance may struggle to afford necessary medications and care.

list.title: Complications:
list.snippet: Individuals with diabetes-related complications (kidney disease, heart disease, vision loss) incur additional expenses.

list.title: Medication Costs:
list.snippet: Insulin and other diabetes medications can be a significant expense, particularly for those with Type 1 diabetes who require insulin.

list.title: Cost-sharing:
list.snippet: Copays, deductibles, and coinsurance can significantly impact out-of-pocket costs.

list.title: Geographic Location:
list.snippet: Some states have implemented insulin copay caps, which can help reduce costs.

list.title: Access to resources:
list.snippet: Patient assistance programs, copay cards, and other resources can help offset the cost of medications.
Insulin: Prices vary widely, but some pharmacies offer affordable options like Walmart's ReliOn insulin for around $25/vial.
Diabetes supplies: Costs for test strips, glucose monitors, and other supplies can add up.
Doctor visits: Regular checkups and consultations with specialists are essential for diabetes management.
Hospitalizations: Severe complications can lead to costly hospital stays.
Lost productivity: Diabetes can impact a person's ability to work, leading to lost wages and reduced income.
